title: My family
goal: Introduce family members and describe people — while noticing a spot where many languages are **more detailed** than Estonian.
bekal: name the members of your immediate and extended family
point to people and things with *see*, *need*, and *too*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Foto telefonis
dialogs.intro: In a shared study room, Budi shows a photo of his family on his phone screen.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Kas see on sinu pere?
lines.id: Is this your family?
lines.literal: is-it this is-it your family?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah, see on foto meie majast Bandungis.
lines.id: Yes, this is a photo of our house in Bandung.
lines.literal: yes, this is-it photo our house-of Bandung-in.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Kes see naine on?
lines.id: Who is this woman?
lines.literal: who this woman is-she?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: See on minu ema. Tema nimi on Sari.
lines.id: That's my mother. Her name is Sari.
lines.literal: that is-she my mother. her name is-it Sari.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ja see mees tema kõrval?
lines.id: And the man next to her?
lines.literal: and this man her next-to?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: See on mu isa, Hasan. Ta on arst.
lines.id: That's my father, Hasan. He's a doctor.
lines.literal: that is-he my father, Hasan. he is-he doctor.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Kas sul on õdesid või vendi?
lines.id: Do you have sisters or brothers?
lines.literal: is-it you-at is sister-plural-(partial) or brother-plural-(partial)?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mul on üks õde ja kaks venda.
lines.id: I have one sister and two brothers.
lines.literal: me-at is one sister and two brother-(partial).

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Kes on see tüdruk?
lines.id: Who is that girl?
lines.literal: who is-she that girl?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: See on mu õde Dewi. Ta on noorem kui mina.
lines.id: That's my younger sister Dewi. She's younger than me.
lines.literal: that is-she my sister Dewi. she is-she more-young than me.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Aa, siis ta on sinu noorem õde.
lines.id: Ah, so she's your little sister.
lines.literal: ah, then she is-she your more-young sister.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah. Aga eesti keeles on ainult "õde", eks?
lines.id: Yes. But in Estonian there's just "õde", right?
lines.literal: yes. but Estonian language-in is only "sister", right?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Täpselt. Meil pole eraldi sõna vanema ja noorema jaoks.
lines.id: Exactly. We have no separate words for older and younger.
lines.literal: exactly. us-at not-is separate word older-of and younger-of for.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Indoneesia keeles on. "Kakak" ja "adik".
lines.id: In Indonesian there are. "Kakak" and "adik".
lines.literal: Indonesian language-in there-is. "kakak" and "adik".

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Huvitav! Meil on ainult "vanem õde" ja "noorem õde".
lines.id: Interesting! We only have "older sister" and "younger sister".
lines.literal: interesting! us-at is only "older sister" and "younger sister".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja kes on see vana mees?
lines.id: And who is that old man?
lines.literal: and who is-he that old man?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ma arvan, et see on sinu vanaisa.
lines.id: I guess that's your grandfather.
lines.literal: I think-I, that that is-he your grandfather.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Õige! Ta on kaheksakümmend aastat vana.
lines.id: Right! He's eighty years old.
lines.literal: right! he is-he eighty year-(partial) old.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ta näeb väga rõõmus välja.
lines.id: He looks very happy.
lines.literal: he looks-he very happy out.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: On küll. Ta on meie pere lemmik.
lines.id: He is. He's our family's favorite.
lines.literal: is indeed. he is-he our family favorite.

notes: ⚠️ **See means "this" and "that" at once.** English separates near from far; everyday Estonian uses *see* for both. Notice how the same word is translated "this" in the first line and "that" in the fourth. There is a word *too* for the far one, but it is rarely used in ordinary conversation.

**Minu ema, mu isa.** Once again a long and a short pair. Kerli and Budi use the long form when introducing someone for the first time and the short form afterwards — not a rigid rule, but that is what sounds natural.
**Tema nimi on Sari**, not "tema on Sari". Estonian says "her name is Sari", not "she is Sari". To give someone else's name, this is the natural structure.
**Mul on üks õde** — literally "at-me is one sister". Estonian has **no verb "to have"** at all. This is covered fully in Unit 4; for now memorize *mul on* = "I have", *sul on* = "you have".

grammars.title: Possessives — minu, sinu, tema
body: Estonian possessives are really ordinary pronouns in their possessive form, and they go **in front of** the noun, just like English "my", "your", "our".
after: Notice that the possessive forms are **almost the same** as the long pronouns from Unit 1 (*mina* → *minu*, *sina* → *sinu*, *tema*, *meie*, *teie*): they are simply those pronouns in the possessive case, so there is no big new table to memorize.
⚠️ *Nende* has no short form. If you need "their", there is only one choice.
The noun **does not change** because of the possessive. *Maja* stays *maja*: *minu maja*, *sinu maja*, *nende maja*. Estonian doesn't attach possessive endings the way Finnish or Turkish does.

grammars.title: See, need, too — pointing
body: Three pointing words, but in everyday conversation you almost always need only the first two.

head: Word
Meaning
Example
Note
rows: ⚠️ Covers near **and** far. This is the one you use.
Rare; used when you really need to tell them apart.

after: *See* is also used as "it/that" for an idea, just like in English: *See on hea.* (That's good.) *See ei ole tõsi.* (That's not true.)

⚠️ Don't confuse it with *ta*. *See* is for things and — in casual conversation — also for a person being pointed at. *Ta* is for a person already being talked about. *Kes see on?* (Who is that?) then *Ta on arst.* (He/she is a doctor.)

English
Note
rows: Two meanings, like "husband/man" in many languages.

blocks.title: ⚠️ No "older/younger" sibling words
items: Estonian is simple here, and works just like English: it **doesn't distinguish older from younger siblings** at all — *õde* is "sister", *vend* is "brother". (Languages such as Indonesian, Chinese, or Korean do make that distinction, which is why Budi's remark in the dialogue is a talking point.)
If you need to, add an adjective: *vanem õde* (older sister), *noorem vend* (younger brother).
But know that Estonians almost never feel the need to say it. If you say *mul on õde*, nobody will ask "older or younger?" — the question simply doesn't feel important.

The same goes for address: there are **no honorific titles** for older people, like "Sir" or "Madam". Estonians call anyone by first name, including people much older than themselves. It takes some getting used to.

blocks.text: Notice the prefix **eba-** in *ebasõbralik*. It works like English "un-" or "in-", and it is productive: *ebamugav* (uncomfortable), *ebaviisakas* (impolite), *ebakindel* (uncertain). If you know the adjective, you know its opposite.

blocks.title: Ready-made patterns
items: *Minu ema on väga sõbralik.* — My mother is very friendly.
*Ta on pikk ja tugev.* — He/she is tall and strong.
*Ta näeb noor välja.* — He/she looks young. (*välja nägema* = to look like; the two parts are separated)
*Ta on noorem kui mina.* — He/she is younger than me.

head: Eesti keel
English
rows: How many children do you have?

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Kui vana ta on?* is literally "how old is he/she", and it is the only way to ask about age. Just like English "how old are you" — Estonian asks about being old, not about "age" as a noun.
To answer: *Ma olen kakskümmend viis aastat vana* (I am twenty-five years old), or shorter and more common, *Ma olen kakskümmend viis*. The numbers themselves are unpacked in Unit 4.
